etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin rēiectus, past participle of reicere (“to throw back”), from re- (“back”) + iacere (“to throw”). Displaced native Old English āweorpan (literally “to throw out”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To refuse to accept; to forswear.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: One morning I had been driven to the precarious refuge afforded by the steps of the inn, after rejecting offers from the Celebrity to join him in a variety of amusements. But even here I was not free from interruption, for he was seated on a horse-block below me, playing with a fox terrier.

definitions.definition: (basketball) To block a shot, especially if it sends the ball off the court.

quote.citation: 2011, Lenka, Ben H. Allen (lyrics and music), “Roll with the Punches”, in Two‎[1], performed by Lenka:
quote.text: It's unexpected / It usually is / When you're rejected / Or you take a hit

quote.citation: 1996, Jim Blinn, Jim Blinn's Corner: A Trip Down the Graphics Pipeline, page 127:
quote.text: Almost all line segments will be trivial accepts or trivial rejects, so the above covers the vast majority of cases.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) A rejected defective product in a production line.

quote.citation: 2001, Salman Rushdie, Fury: A Novel, London: Jonathan Cape, →ISBN, page 6:
quote.text: In all of India, China, Africa, and much of the southern American continent, those who had the leisure and wallet for fashion  […]  would have killed for the street merchandise of Manhattan, as also for  […]  the reject china and designer-label bargains to be found in downtown discount emporia.
